name: Albanian
variety: Standard Albanian, which is based on Tosk; phonetic detail from Northern Tosk speakers (Coretta et al. 2023)
sources: Coretta, Stefano; Riverin-Coutlée, Josiane; Kapia, Enkeleida; Nichols, Stephen (2023). Northern Tosk Albanian. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 53(3): 1122-1144.
Newmark, Leonard; Hubbard, Philip; Prifti, Peter (1982). Standard Albanian: A Reference Grammar for Students. Stanford University Press.
Buchholz, Oda; Fiedler, Wilfried (1987). Albanische Grammatik. Leipzig: Verlag Enzyklopädie.
Camaj, Martin (1984). Albanian Grammar. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz.
Moosmüller, Sylvia; Granser, Theodor (2006). The spread of Standard Albanian: an illustration based on an analysis of vowels. Language Variation and Change 18: 121-140.
Kolgjini, Julie M. (2004). Palatalization in Albanian: an acoustic investigation of stops and affricates. PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Arlington.
contrasts: two rhotics: a tap or flap (written r) against a trill (written rr)
two laterals: a plain, slightly palatalised alveolar /l/ against a velarised dental /ɫ/ (written ll)
dental fricatives /θ ð/ beside /s z/ and /ʃ ʒ/
three pairs of affricates: alveolar /t͡s d͡z/, postalveolar /t͡ʃ d͡ʒ/, and the pair written q, gj, traditionally palatal stops /c ɟ/
voicing in all stops, affricates and fricatives except /h/
front rounded /y/ and a mid central vowel (written ë) that can be stressed
no contrast of vowel length or nasality in the Tosk-based standard; both exist in Gheg
allophony: q and gj are affricates for Northern Tosk speakers, with a laminal postalveolar closure; they are never plain stops in the JIPA recordings, and they merge with /t͡ʃ d͡ʒ/ in many Gheg varieties
the single r is a tap, often a retroflex flap [ɽ] or approximant [ɻ], the approximant mostly in a syllable coda
/ɫ/ may be vocalised in running speech
the vowel written ë is more open than a schwa, near [ɜ], with slight lip rounding; /y/ is a lax [ʏ]; /a/ is central to back
final unstressed ë is weak and often dropped in colloquial speech
voiceless stops are unaspirated, /k/ with a longer release; voiced stops are fully prevoiced
voiced obstruents at the end of a word are often devoiced in colloquial Tosk
phonotactics: initial clusters of nasal plus stop (mb, nd, ng, ngj) and of sh or zh plus consonant (shk, shp, zgj)
the mid central vowel is frequent in unstressed syllables, before and after the stress
vowel sequences such as ie, ua, ye are common; whether they are diphthongs or two syllables is disputed

stress.type: lexical, largely predictable from word structure
stress.rule: Stress falls on the last syllable of the stem: on the final syllable of most consonant-final words and of many vowel-final ones (liri, shtëpi, atdhe), on the penultimate of words ending in unstressed -ë, -e, -ër, -ur and the like; endings and the suffixed article do not move it, so it can stand on the antepenultimate of an inflected form (flutura).
stress.cues: stressed vowels are longer and higher in pitch; intensity is a less regular cue (Coretta et al. 2023)

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: unstressed ë is short and may drop; other unstressed vowels keep their quality
rhythm.notes: No rhythm-metric study was found. Word-final vowels tend to be lengthened (noted by Coretta et al. 2023).

length.notes: No phonemic length in the standard language. Gheg varieties contrast short and long (in the north-west also extra-long) vowels.

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Coretta et al. 2023, table 1 (five speakers, word-initial stops in isolated words, 15 tokens per word)

intonation.yes_no_question: rising contour; the question is often introduced by the particle a
intonation.wh_question: rising in the recordings of Coretta et al. (2023); earlier descriptions also give questions a rising contour
intonation.continuation: not described in the sources consulted
intonation.accent_shape: higher pitch on the stressed syllable
intonation.notes: Recent work links topic, information focus and contrastive focus to different tunes in Standard Albanian; the details were not checked.

problems: a word-final vowel is never stressed unless a rule says so: shtëpi, liri, atdhe and kafe are stressed on the penultimate syllable, in shtëpi even on ë
rr at the beginning of a word gets a schwa in front (rrugë is given as [əˈruɡə])
single r is a trill and rr a double trill, so the contrast is one of length, not tap against trill
the vowel sequences ua and ie are made a glide plus vowel (grua as [ɡrwɑ], dielli as [djelli]), which moves the syllable peak
final unstressed ë after a consonant is made a very short schwa by rule in most words, a colloquial feature applied everywhere
IPA output is misleading: plain l is printed [ɫ], velarised ll is printed 'll', and stressed ë is printed [ʌ]
no voicing of /h/ between vowels and no sandhi across words
good: l and ll are distinct sounds with clear and dark formant patterns
q and gj are alveolo-palatal affricates, close to the Northern Tosk realisation
dental fricatives, /y/ and the three affricate pairs are present
suffix rules keep the stress on the stem in inflected forms (punëtor, tavolinë, universitet, faleminderit are correct)

notes: Vowel formants are left out: Coretta et al. (2023) give only a normalised F1/F2 plot, and the values of Moosmüller & Granser (2006) could not be checked.
